value.overview: The Tennessee Warbler (Leiothlypis peregrina) is a small New World wood-warbler that breeds in the boreal forests of Canada and Alaska and migrates through the United States to winter in Central and northern South America. Despite its common name, it is not associated with Tennessee as a breeding bird. It is especially notable for feeding heavily on spruce budworm caterpillars during population outbreaks. In Costa Rica, it is a seasonal migrant rather than a resident species.
value.classification: The Tennessee Warbler belongs to the family Parulidae, the New World warblers. Its accepted scientific name is Leiothlypis peregrina; it was formerly placed in the genus Vermivora.
value.identification: This is a small, slim warbler with a thin, pointed bill and relatively long wings. Adults commonly show an olive-green back, pale underparts, a yellowish or whitish throat, and two pale wing bars. The head pattern varies with age and plumage, but many birds show a pale eyebrow, dark eye line, and grayish crown or face markings. Fall migrants can appear duller and more greenish, making identification more difficult. Its active movements and sharp, slender bill are useful field clues.
value.rangeHabitat: The Tennessee Warbler breeds mainly in spruce and fir forests across boreal Canada and Alaska. It migrates through much of the eastern and central United States and winters from southern Mexico through Central America to northern South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs as a regular but seasonal migrant, chiefly during autumn and spring passage, and may also remain through the northern winter. It uses forest edges, second growth, shrubby clearings, gardens, coffee plantations, and both lowland and montane wooded habitats.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica it is present mainly from roughly September through April, with passage birds occurring in both spring and autumn; it is not normally a year-round resident.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in the northern boreal forest, especially in spruce-dominated habitats. The female builds a small cup nest low in dense vegetation, often near the ground, using plant fibers and other fine materials. A clutch commonly contains several eggs, which are incubated primarily by the female. Both adults feed the young. Breeding success and local abundance can increase sharply during outbreaks of spruce budworm, an important food source during the nesting season.
value.dietFeeding: During the breeding season, the Tennessee Warbler feeds largely on caterpillars and other insects, especially spruce budworm larvae when available. It also takes moths, beetles, flies, aphids, spiders, and other small invertebrates. On migration and in winter, it supplements this diet with berries, small fruits, and nectar. It usually forages actively among leaves and twigs, sometimes hovering briefly or joining mixed-species feeding flocks.
value.behavior: This warbler is active and mobile, often moving through foliage with quick hops and short flights. It may forage alone, in pairs during the breeding season, or in mixed flocks with other small insect-eating birds during migration and winter. Males sing from concealed perches in breeding habitat, while migrants are generally quieter. Its abundance can vary considerably between years because populations respond to changes in spruce budworm availability and breeding-season conditions.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered to be declining, despite strong natural fluctuations associated with spruce budworm outbreaks. Long-term monitoring indicates that conservation attention is warranted, particularly across migratory and wintering areas.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include loss and degradation of forest habitat on the breeding grounds and along migration routes, conversion of natural vegetation in Central and South America, pesticide exposure, and climate-driven changes affecting boreal forests and insect populations. Habitat loss in Costa Rica and elsewhere can reduce the quality of stopover and wintering sites.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect mature and regenerating boreal forest, native woodland, forest edges, and other habitats used during migration and winter. In Costa Rica, retaining shade trees, native vegetation, forest corridors, and diverse vegetation around farms and gardens can benefit this and other migratory birds. Avoid unnecessary insecticide use, support habitat-friendly coffee and agriculture, and report sightings through well-managed bird-monitoring programs.
